In some surprisingly great news the Freedom Act, the Patriot Act's brother, has failed to even make it to vote by a vote of 57-42. The patriot act provisions were set to expire and ending debate on the motion enabling the senators to bring it to an up or down vote would have required 60 votes. That did not happen so it's basically done with. What I didn't expect was the partisan distribution.

Voting for bringing the Freedom Act to vote = 12 republican, 44 democrat, 1 independent

Voting against bringing the Freedom Act to vote = 41 republican, 0 democrat, 1 independent

The thing that made me bother to look this up is that the news organizations reporting on this including sites like The Guardian, The Verge, and so on are atypically not including the partisan breakdown of the vote. I'm assuming I'm simply missing something here as even individuals like Mitch McConnell voted against this motion, whereas Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren voted for it. What's going on?
Why was the "Freedom Act" being nearly exclusively supported by democrats in the senate?

That might be just a bit hyperbolic. In general both parties have been pushing fairly hard for domestic surveillance and spying powers. Mitch McConnell in particular is something like the poster-boy for NSA activism. At least to me this vote distribution is completely incomprehensible and the media is as useless as usual when it comes to actually meaningfully describing the news.
But the question wasn't about the republicans it was why are the democrats doing this.

Ah fair point. Perhaps I chose a poor title. I'm mostly interested in what caused this vote distribution in general. I don't think Rand Paul has that much clout, and McConnell also voting against it just boggles my mind. I'm certain there's some sort of political underpinning here that I'm simply missing. I was hoping somebody more informed than myself could chime in.

If we look at the history of USA Patriot Act, it was first proposed and supported almost unanimously by Republicans, with overwhelming Democratic support. As the re-authorizations came up, Republicans continued to support it nearly unanimously, while Democrats became less likely to support it. (After the 2010 election, Tea Party Republicans has the highest rate of support. So much for their campaign promises!)

Today, we have this situation where Obama and the Republicans want to maintain the Act or at least maintain most of it in the "compromise." Although this seems like a strange alignment now, this was routine during the Clinton years.

If nothing is done, spying laws automatically expire on June 1.

Republicans want to avoid a vote so that they won't be tied down to having to explain voting for the Patriot Act which is now very unpopular. Democrats want to force a vote so they can make Republicans to take a stand on the record. It's an old trick.

This is not about support or opposition for Patriot directly; it is about exposing positions on the record.

Since many in the Senate want to extend the Patriot Act, the negotiations are going to become intense. Right now, it doesn't look good for the Act. Expect to see more twists and turns this week.
And that sounds exactly like that underpinning I was missing. Much appreciated.

What do you think was good about the patriot act? From my perspective it took one huge step forward in turning the US into a surveillance state at the cost of billions of dollars. Ironically that surveillance has shown itself to be less than useful. Even the agencies who were utilizing the spying powers it granted have now acknowledged that it didn't help crack any major cases. We had a major act of domestic terrorism from a couple of kids who were anything but subtle, yet caught all intelligence agencies with their pants down. This is made even worse by the fact that Russia specifically warned the FBI about one of the brothers in this case.

I would also oppose the surveillance even had it shown to be effective given Franklin's famous old quote, "He who would give up essential liberty to purchase a little temporary safety, deserve neither liberty nor safety." But the fact that it's not even effective makes it completely indefensible in my opinion. Whichever loopholes you're mentioning should be brought to the forefront and squashed, not formally endorsed and regulated by secret courts who are publicly accountable to nobody and allowed to silence dissent or calls to accountability under the all encompassing guise of "national security."

What part of the patriot act has personally stomped on your freedom? Any actual personal accounts?

Anyone?

If you have nothing to hide then what part of the Patriot act concerns you?

I've heard this argument before, and I strongly disagree with the concept "if you have nothing to hide". Our justice system is simply not built on this concept. Certainly, and you've probably read them, we can take this to levels of the ridiculous level: if we have nothing to hide why have walls? why not submit our travel schedule to a government representative each day? I don't think these arguments are anything profound, but equally I don't think "if you have nothing to hide" is a sound argument in favor of mass surveillance.

Next, the first part of your argument is based on the concept of some personal effect being requisite for concern. On the premise, I disagree here.There are many things I'm concerned about that don't directly effect me. However, and I think this is one of the primary reasons for the secrecy element, it would very difficult to expound on specific ways our freedoms have been impugned. In my opinion, this secrecy does not prevent criticism though.

Governments being in open control of massive amounts of private information is incredibly dangerous. The people in charge of this information are only human. Snowden is a perfect example. We are lucky he was a "good guy." In another time and place he could have been a greedy treacherous individual and simply collected all the possible private information he could and then sold it to the highest bidder, or sold it to all of them for that matter.

It also opens the door to sanctioned abuse. Since the governments engaged in this sort of domestic spying are able to hide their exact methods, data, and other information under the guise of "national security" you and I are basically left to take their word when they claim to have collected certain information about an individual. What's to stop them from fabricating things about an individual that somebody in power decides is undesirable? Nothing. This sort of system has no built in check and balance and it complete stomps all over the 4th amendment.

Next illegal does not necessarily mean unethical, nor does legal inherently mean right or just. There was a time when a black person refusing to give up their seat to a white person would have been a crime. Organizing a protest involving this specific act would have been a conspiracy charge on top of it. Turning our country into a surveillance state allows unjust laws to be ruthlessly enforced without fear of organized opposition.

And of course even today you do have something to hide even if you don't realize it. Give me access to everything you've ever done or said and I assure you you have broken some laws somewhere. The law in the US is absurdly bloated. There are tens of thousands of statutes and clauses many of which are completely absurd in modern times yet remain on the books largely because nobody ever bothered to take them off. Once again getting back to the sanctioned abuse, that doesn't mean these laws couldn't suddenly spring into action to get rid of an undesired individual. For instance a number of the Occupy protesters in New York were arrested based on a 150 year old law which prohibits wearing masks in public gatherings. Little did they know publicly wearing a Guy Fawkes mask was illegal. And little do you know all the numerous nuanced little laws you've undoubtedly broken.

I guessing there are 3 different camps in the congress right now. 1) Keep the patriot act; 2) Replace it with the freedom act; 3) Scrap them both; Groups 1 and 2 would make the obvious choices on the vote but group 3 are going to fall into 2 separate groups. Those who believe they can get rid of the patriot act without the freedom act and those that see the freedom act as the lesser of 2 evils and believe the votes aren't there to get rid of both the patriot act and the freedom act.
